levels.6.title: The meeting point
levels.6.intro: Lines don't just cross: they meet at points called vertices. There, and only there, the interaction happens. This is an isolated vertex: the basic piece of every diagram.
levels.6.steps.find.prompt: Tap the vertex in the diagram.
levels.6.steps.find.wrongDefault: That point is an endpoint: a particle coming in or going out. The vertex is where the lines join.
levels.6.steps.find.hints.0: Look for the point where several lines come together.
levels.6.steps.find.hints.1: It's the bright point in the middle.
levels.6.steps.find.solved: That's the vertex: the place where the interaction happens.
levels.6.steps.count.prompt: How many lines meet at this vertex?
levels.6.steps.count.options.3.feedback: Three lines: always three in QED.
levels.6.steps.count.options.4.feedback: Count again the lines reaching the central point.
levels.6.steps.count.hints.0: Count the lines touching the central point.
levels.6.steps.count.hints.1: There are two straight ones and one wavy one.
levels.6.steps.rule.prompt: Which combination of lines forms a QED vertex?
levels.6.steps.rule.options.qed.text: Two fermion lines (one arrow in and one out) and a photon
levels.6.steps.rule.options.qed.feedback: This is QED's only interaction rule.
levels.6.steps.rule.options.photons.feed: Photons have no charge: they don't interact directly with each other in QED.
levels.6.steps.rule.options.electrons.fe: Charge wouldn't be conserved, and in QED the interaction always goes through a photon.
levels.6.steps.rule.hints.0: Look at which kinds of line touch the vertex.
levels.6.steps.rule.hints.1: One of the arrows arrives at the vertex and the other leaves it.
levels.6.success: You've discovered QED's fundamental rule: one vertex, three lines.
levels.6.explanation.intuitive: An electron can emit or absorb a photon. All of electricity, magnetism and light comes from this single rule.
levels.6.explanation.scientific: The QED vertex couples the electron field to the photon field. It always joins one incoming fermion line, one outgoing fermion line and one photon line. The same vertex, rotated, describes emission, absorption, annihilation or pair creation.
levels.6.explanation.math: Each vertex contributes a factor −ieγ^μ, where e is the elementary charge and γ^μ are the Dirac matrices.
levels.7.title: The arrow doesn't break
levels.7.intro: Now it's your turn to build. At each vertex, the arrow that comes in must carry on going out. That's how charge conservation is drawn.
levels.7.steps.out-electron.prompt: Complete the vertex: the electron must leave on the right. Drag from the vertex to the exit point.
levels.7.steps.out-electron.hints.0: The arrow follows the direction of your gesture.
levels.7.steps.out-electron.hints.1: An outgoing electron has its arrow pointing right: drag from the vertex outward.
levels.7.steps.out-electron.solved: The arrow comes in and goes out: charge is conserved.
levels.7.steps.in-positron.prompt: A positron comes in at the bottom and meets an electron. Draw the positron's line with the correct arrow.
levels.7.steps.in-positron.hints.0: An incoming positron has its arrow pointing against time.
levels.7.steps.in-positron.hints.1: Drag from the vertex to the entry point at the bottom: that way the arrow points left.
levels.7.success: You've drawn charge conservation with a simple arrow.
levels.7.explanation.intuitive: What comes in on one side goes out on the other: the arrow is never cut or duplicated.
levels.7.explanation.scientific: Arrows form continuous lines that pass through the vertices. This expresses conservation of fermion number and, in QED, of electric charge. An incoming electron (−1) and an incoming positron (+1) add up to 0, the photon's charge.
levels.7.explanation.math: Charge conservation follows from QED's U(1) gauge symmetry (Noether's theorem). At each vertex, the current ψ̄γ^μψ is conserved.
levels.8.title: Impossible vertices
levels.8.intro: A lab engineer has drawn some diagrams with mistakes. Use the rules you know to find what's wrong.
levels.8.steps.four.prompt: This vertex connects two electrons and two photons. What's wrong with it as a fundamental vertex?
levels.8.steps.four.options.three.text: A QED vertex joins exactly three lines: two fermion lines and a photon
levels.8.steps.four.options.three.feedba: There is no fundamental four-line vertex in QED.
levels.8.steps.four.options.fine.text: Nothing: a vertex can have as many photons as it likes
levels.8.steps.four.options.fine.feedbac: QED has only one kind of vertex, with exactly one photon.
levels.8.steps.four.options.emit.feedbac: They can: that's exactly what a correct three-line vertex describes.
levels.8.steps.four.hints.0: Count the lines at the vertex.
levels.8.steps.four.hints.1: The rule from level 6: three lines, one of them a photon.
levels.8.steps.four.solved: That process exists, but it's drawn with two chained vertices, not with one four-line vertex.
levels.8.steps.fix-flow.prompt: In this diagram one vertex violates charge conservation. Tap the culprit line and flip its arrow.
levels.8.steps.fix-flow.hints.0: Check the arrows vertex by vertex: at each one, one must come in and another go out.
levels.8.steps.fix-flow.hints.1: Two arrows come into the top vertex. The editable line is the top exit.
levels.8.success: You spot vertices that nature doesn't allow. You're the lab's quality control.
levels.8.explanation.intuitive: QED has only one interaction rule. If a drawing breaks it, it doesn't describe anything that can happen.
levels.8.explanation.scientific: The QED Lagrangian contains only one interaction term, ψ̄γ^μψA_μ, with two fermion fields and one photon. That's why there's a single fundamental three-line vertex. Processes like e⁻γ → e⁻γ (Compton) are described by chaining two vertices.
levels.8.explanation.math: A term with two photons and two electrons would have mass dimension 5 and make the theory non-renormalizable. It doesn't appear in QED.
levels.9.title: Allowed isn't possible
levels.9.intro: A correct vertex is a valid piece of the language. But can it happen on its own in nature? Here physics sets you a little trap.
levels.9.steps.emission.prompt: This vertex follows the rules of QED. Can a free, isolated electron emit a real photon like this, with nothing else?
levels.9.steps.emission.options.no.text: No: it can't conserve both energy and momentum
levels.9.steps.emission.options.no.feedb: In the rest frame of the initial electron, there's no energy available to create a photon.
levels.9.steps.emission.options.yes.text: Yes: electrons emit light all the time
levels.9.steps.emission.options.yes.feed: Electrons emit light when they interact with something (a nucleus, a field, another electron). A lone electron in vacuum can't.
levels.9.steps.emission.hints.0: Imagine the electron at rest before emitting.
levels.9.steps.emission.hints.1: Where would the photon's energy come from if the electron can't lose mass?
levels.9.steps.pair.prompt: And a lone photon in vacuum? Can it turn into an electron and a positron?
levels.9.steps.pair.options.needs.text: Not on its own: it needs another particle nearby, such as a nucleus, to absorb momentum
levels.9.steps.pair.options.needs.feedba: That's why pair creation is seen when a high-energy photon passes close to a nucleus.
levels.9.steps.pair.options.energy.text: Yes, if it has enough energy
levels.9.steps.pair.options.energy.feedb: Not even with all the energy in the world. In the frame where the pair has zero total momentum, the photon would need zero momentum and non-zero energy, which is impossible for a photon.
levels.9.steps.pair.hints.0: A photon always moves at the speed of light and always has momentum.
levels.9.steps.pair.hints.1: The e⁻e⁺ pair can be at rest as a whole; the photon never can.
levels.9.steps.meaning.prompt: So what's an isolated vertex good for?
levels.9.steps.meaning.options.piece.tex: It's a piece: real processes are built by combining vertices
levels.9.steps.meaning.options.piece.fee: With two or more vertices, the internal lines can be virtual and the process can happen.
levels.9.steps.meaning.options.useless.t: Nothing: it's a flaw in the formalism
levels.9.steps.meaning.options.useless.f: It's the piece everything else is built from.
levels.9.steps.meaning.hints.1: In the next chapter you'll combine two vertices.
levels.9.success: You've learned a subtlety that confuses many students: allowed doesn't mean possible.
levels.9.explanation.intuitive: The drawing rules say which pieces exist. Conservation laws say which complete processes can really happen.
levels.9.explanation.scientific: A formally allowed diagram doesn't guarantee that the process can happen with real external particles. Three-particle processes with free particles in QED (e → eγ, γ → e⁺e⁻, e⁺e⁻ → γ) violate conservation of four-momentum. Inside bigger diagrams, virtual internal lines get around this restriction.
levels.9.explanation.math: For e(p) → e(p′) + γ(k): (p − k)² = m² implies m² − 2p·k = m², that is, p·k = 0. But for a massive electron and a real photon with positive energy, p·k > 0. Contradiction.
levels.10.title: Design your vertex
levels.10.intro: The same vertex, rotated, describes different processes. Build two versions from scratch, as pieces of bigger diagrams.
levels.10.steps.pair.prompt: Build the vertex where a photon turns into an electron (top) and a positron (bottom).
levels.10.steps.pair.hints.0: The photon first: pick the wavy line and join it to the vertex.
levels.10.steps.pair.hints.1: Outgoing electron: from the vertex outward. Outgoing positron: from outside toward the vertex.
levels.10.steps.pair.solved: Pair creation: a continuous arrow that “turns around” at the vertex.
levels.10.steps.positron.prompt: Now a positron that emits a photon and carries on.
levels.10.steps.positron.hints.0: The positron comes in and goes out: both arrows point against time.
levels.10.steps.positron.hints.1: Drag from the exit to the vertex and from the vertex to the entry.
levels.10.success: You've discovered crossing symmetry: a single vertex, many stories.
levels.10.explanation.intuitive: Rotate the vertex and what was an emission becomes a pair creation. It's the same rule seen from another angle.
levels.10.explanation.scientific: Crossing symmetry relates processes in which an incoming particle is replaced by its outgoing antiparticle. Emission, absorption, annihilation and pair creation are the same vertex with different orientations with respect to time.
levels.10.explanation.math: The amplitudes of crossed processes are obtained by analytic continuation, changing p → −p for the crossed particle.
